data.name: AudioOverlayParagraph1
data.value: Every dot is a real bus. Dozens of them, maybe more, moving through a city that never agreed on a grid. They follow Peachtree and Cascade and Memorial Drive, routes drawn around what Atlanta actually is rather than what a planner imagined.

data.name: AudioOverlayParagraph2
data.value: This is an audio experience — turn your device's sound on. The harmony is slow and syncopated. A note lands where the vehicle happens to be along its route — deep in Vine City, crossing the connector, idling at Edgewood-Candler Park. Morning fills the piece with movement; after midnight the map goes quiet and the notes stretch out. What is playing right now has not played before.

data.name: AudioOverlayParagraph3
data.value: MARTA runs on faith. You wait, and then it comes. This is the music inside that waiting.

data.name: WmataAudioOverlayParagraph1
data.value: Every dot is a real bus or train. Hundreds of them, spread across a city that was planned on a diagonal and then grew past every boundary. They follow Wisconsin and Georgia and Benning Road, and the Red Line arcing through Bethesda, routes drawn around three jurisdictions that never quite agreed on anything.

data.name: WmataAudioOverlayParagraph2
data.value: This is an audio experience — turn your device's sound on. The harmony shifts with the system. A note lands where the vehicle happens to be along its route — transferring at Metro Center, crossing the Anacostia, moving through Silver Spring at rush hour. Commuter peaks fill the piece with density; late nights thin it out to something sparse and unhurried. What is playing right now has not played before.

data.name: WmataAudioOverlayParagraph3
data.value: WMATA connects a capital to itself. Across DC, Maryland, and Virginia, something is always moving. This is the music inside that motion.

data.name: MbtaAudioOverlayParagraph1
data.value: Every dot is a real bus or train. Hundreds of them, spread across a region that grew outward from a harbor and never stopped. They follow Massachusetts Avenue and Blue Hill and the Riverside Line, routes drawn around Boston, Cambridge, Somerville, and the towns reaching out to Providence and Newburyport.

data.name: MbtaAudioOverlayParagraph2
data.value: This is an audio experience — turn your device's sound on. The harmony follows the system. A note lands where the vehicle happens to be along its route — surfacing at Park Street, crossing the Charles, moving through Roxbury at rush hour. The Red, Orange, and Blue lines weave through the piece alongside hundreds of buses. What is playing right now has not played before.

data.name: MbtaAudioOverlayParagraph3
data.value: The T is the oldest subway in America. It carries the city forward on the same lines it always has. This is the music inside that motion.

data.name: MbtaOverlayParagraph1
data.value: Every dot is a real MBTA vehicle, pulled live and turned into sound. Buses and trains — including the Red, Orange, and Blue lines — move through Greater Boston in real time, and the map plays what they're doing right now.

data.name: TtcAudioOverlayParagraph1
data.value: Every dot is a real bus or streetcar. Hundreds of them, threading a city built on a grid until the ravines cut through it. They follow King and Queen and Dundas and Spadina — the streetcar lines Toronto never gave up — and Eglinton and Jane and Bathurst further out, where the grid finally wins.

data.name: TtcAudioOverlayParagraph2
data.value: This is an audio experience — turn your device's sound on. The harmony rides low and steady, streetcar tracks worn into it like the rails themselves. A note lands where the vehicle happens to be along its route — turning onto Spadina, running the Queen line end to end, waiting out a light on King. Rush hour thickens the piece into something dense and overlapping; late at night it thins to a single streetcar bell in the quiet. What is playing right now has not played before.

data.name: TtcAudioOverlayParagraph3
data.value: Toronto runs the largest streetcar network in the Americas, and it still owns the old downtown lines outright. The subway draws its shape on the map but keeps its own counsel here — the surface is where this city actually speaks. This is the music inside that motion.

data.name: NymtaAudioOverlayParagraph1
data.value: Every dot is a real NYCT vehicle, thousands of them, and most of them are trains. The 7 curls above Queens toward Flushing, the A runs express down Manhattan's west side into Far Rockaway, the 2 and 3 climb through Harlem, the L cuts straight across 14th Street and under the river into Brooklyn, the F swings out over the Culver viaduct. Under all of it, buses fill in every block a tunnel skips — but this is a subway city, and the subway carries it.

data.name: NymtaAudioOverlayParagraph2
data.value: This is an audio experience — turn your device's sound on. A note lands where the vehicle happens to be along its route — but a subway car never says exactly where it is between stations, so its note is inferred, pinned at each platform and drifting along the drawn track until the next one. Express trains skip local stops and their notes leap ahead; the local fills the spaces between. Buses report their own GPS block by block and thread through underneath. What is playing right now has not played before.

data.name: NymtaAudioOverlayParagraph3
data.value: The trains run all night, every night — the only lines in this project that never sleep. When the streets go quiet, the subway is still down there moving under them. This is the music inside that motion.
